chief_complaint: intense fear and blushing during public speaking and eating in restaurants leading to severe occupational avoidance
hpi_details: He is a 27-year-old accountant declining a promotion that requires presentations because of intense anxiety, tremor, blushing, and fear of humiliation. He has not yet started treatment; CBT is preferred, with medication considered after assessment.
ideas: He thinks he has social anxiety.
concerns: He fears embarrassment and that anxiety will limit his career.
expectations: He hopes to receive practical behavioral techniques or a targeted medication to prevent blushing and trembling during presentations.

clinical_knowledge.topic: Social anxiety disorder: evaluation and management
core_concepts: Social anxiety disorder is marked by persistent fear of negative evaluation in social or performance situations, with avoidance or marked distress.
Assess onset, breadth of feared situations, impairment, panic symptoms, depression, substance use, and suicide risk.
Individual CBT with exposure is first-line; SSRIs or SNRIs may be considered when symptoms are persistent or CBT is unavailable or insufficient.

A beta-blocker can sometimes be considered for circumscribed performance anxiety only after checking cardiovascular and respiratory contraindications; it is not a general treatment for social anxiety disorder.
diagnostic_clues: Chief Complaint: intense fear and blushing during public speaking and eating in restaurants leading to severe occupational avoidance
Key HPI features: fear of humiliation, autonomic anxiety symptoms, avoidance of presentations and restaurants, and occupational impairment.
Objective/Exam findings: Mental-state examination, vital signs, and targeted examination or tests only when an alternative medical or substance-related cause is suspected.
Relevant background/PMH: No significant chronic medical history
common_misconceptions: Confusing social anxiety disorder with ordinary shyness when avoidance causes significant impairment.
Assuming all panic-like symptoms are panic disorder without identifying social triggers.
Using alcohol, benzodiazepines, or unsupervised medication as coping strategies.
Overlooking depression, suicidality, or avoidant personality traits.
dangerous_errors: Missing suicidal intent, severe depression, psychosis, intoxication, or withdrawal requiring urgent assessment.
Prescribing a beta-blocker without checking pulse, blood pressure, asthma, diabetes risks, and interacting medicines.
Using benzodiazepines as routine long-term treatment.
management_principles: Offer CBT with graded exposure and address avoidance and safety behaviours.
Assess and treat comorbid depression, other anxiety disorders, and substance misuse.
Discuss SSRI or SNRI treatment with monitoring for adverse effects and early activation when indicated.
Create a safety plan and arrange urgent evaluation for suicidal intent, inability to stay safe, psychosis, or severe substance-related symptoms.
boundaries_and_exceptions: Specific drug dosages, monitoring protocols, and referral criteria must be tailored to organ function, comorbidities, and local hospital pathways.
Atypical presentations in elderly, pediatric, or immunocompromised patients may require lower thresholds for inpatient monitoring and specialist consultation.

reference_soap.subjective: He reports marked fear of embarrassment, blushing, and trembling when speaking publicly or eating in restaurants, leading him to decline a promotion.
reference_soap.objective: Perform mental-state examination, assess function, depression, substance use, and suicide risk, and check vital signs. Investigate medical contributors only if history or examination indicates them.
reference_soap.assessment: Social anxiety disorder is likely, with performance and broader social triggers; assess for panic disorder, depression, substance-related anxiety, and avoidant personality disorder.
reference_soap.plan: Offer CBT with exposure. Discuss an SSRI or SNRI if indicated and monitor response and adverse effects. Consider a beta-blocker only for isolated performance situations after contraindication screening. Urgently escalate for suicidal intent, psychosis, or inability to remain safe.

teaching.one_liner: Psychiatric evaluation for patient presenting with intense fear and blushing during public speaking and eating in restaurants leading to severe occupational avoidance.

must_ask.say: What happens when you have to speak in front of others or eat in a restaurant?
Do you notice blushing, trembling, or sweating in these situations?
Are you afraid people will judge or embarrass you in front of others?
Have you turned down opportunities, like a promotion, to avoid these situations?
How long have you had this fear, and has it gotten worse over time?

history.answer: I get intensely nervous whenever I have to speak in front of others or even eat in public places.
It happens whenever I have to give presentations at work, speak up in meetings, or eat lunch in restaurants around other people.
I have felt shy and uncomfortable around groups since my late teens, but it has become much worse and debilitating over the past two years.
It is not constant, and it does not come out of nowhere; it spikes rapidly right before and during those specific social or speaking situations.
My face blushes intensely red, my hands start shaking, and my heart beats very fast.
I feel tense and my chest tightens when I have to speak, but I do not feel like I am suffocating or dying.
I am terrified that people will notice my blushing and trembling hands and judge me as incompetent or foolish.
I spend days dreading upcoming meetings, and I deliberately avoid public eating areas and speaking up in group settings.
I do not have constant worries about everyday things like money or health, and I am not generally restless or tense at home.
It is severely affecting my career; I just declined a major promotion at my accounting firm because it requires client presentations.
history.topic: Impact on work and daily life

history.answer: Being offered the promotion and pressured to present financial reports was the main stressor that made me realize I need help.
No, I have never experienced any traumatic events or nightmares, and I do not have repetitive rituals or intrusive thoughts.
I feel down and frustrated about missing out on the promotion, but I still enjoy my personal hobbies when I am by myself.
No, I have never had any thoughts of hurting myself or ending my life.
No, my weight has been completely stable, and I do not have heat intolerance or sweating when I am resting.
No, I have never had chest pain while exercising, and I have never passed out.
I drink just one cup of black coffee in the morning, and I do not drink energy drinks.
I only drink a glass of beer once or twice a month, and I never use alcohol to calm my nerves.
I do not take sleeping pills, sedatives, or any illicit drugs.
I have tried deep breathing exercises and sitting in the back of meeting rooms, but I have never sought professional treatment before.
I did some research online, and I think I might have social anxiety disorder.
I am terrified of embarrassing myself and that this anxiety will permanently derail my career advancement.
I'm hoping to get concrete exercises or maybe a pill to take before big meetings so my face doesn't flush and my hands stop shaking.
I do not have any chronic medical conditions or past illnesses.
I have never had surgery and I have never been hospitalized.
I do not take any prescription medications, over-the-counter medicines, or dietary supplements.
I do not have any known allergies to medications, foods, or other substances.
I have never smoked cigarettes or used any tobacco or vaping products.
I work as an accountant and live alone in an apartment near my office.
My father has always been very shy and avoids social events, but no one in the family has a diagnosed psychiatric disorder.

exam.finding: He appears mildly anxious and hesitant with modest eye contact, but is neatly groomed, calm, and cooperative throughout.
Blood pressure is 122/78 mmHg, pulse 76 beats per minute, respiratory rate 14 breaths per minute, oxygen saturation 99% on room air, and temperature 36.6 degrees Celsius.
He is alert and oriented to person, place, and time, with fluent speech, logical thought processes, an anxious mood, and no suicidal ideation or perceptual disturbances.
Thyroid gland is normal in size, non-tender, smooth, and symmetrical, without palpable nodules or bruits.
No resting, postural, or kinetic hand tremor is observed during the examination.
Pupils are equal, round, and reactive to light, with no exophthalmos, lid lag, or abnormal eye movements.
Regular rate and rhythm with normal first and second heart sounds, and no murmurs, rubs, or gallops heard.
Clear breath sounds bilaterally across all lung fields with no wheezes, crackles, or rhonchi.
